newsitem.title: USA: U.S. study finds some blood donors lie about risks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. study finds some blood donors lie about risks.

text.p: An anonymous survey of U.S. blood donors found that some lied at the time they gave blood when asked about risky behaviors that made them susceptible to AIDS and other infections, researchers said on Tuesday.

Of 35,000 blood donors from five cities who responded to the survey created by American Red Cross Blood Services in Baltimore, nearly 2 percent later admitted to risk factors that would have disqualified them from giving blood.
Nearly one-half of 1 percent of the donors reported that the risky behaviors occurred within the previous three months of giving blood.

The Red Cross' Alan Williams, writing in the Journal of the American Medical Association, said that the United States' blood supply was safe, and that all donated blood was screened against infectious diseases, including AIDS, hepatitis B and C and syphilis.
A combination of donor screening and laboratory testing has reduced the risk of transmitting HIV through blood transfusion to an estimated two per one million units of blood, he wrote.
"(But) our study shows that only 8.2 percent of those who reported risks were screened out for laboratory testing," Williams wrote.

"While the prevalence of deferrable risk factors is low, the public health consequences of these observations are substantial considering the fact that 12 million donations ... are drawn annually in the United States," he wrote.

The risk factors for contracting a blood-borne disease included intravenous drug use, sex with an intravenous drug user, sex with a prostitute of either gender, men having sex with other men at any time since 1977, a history of syphilis or gonorrhea in the past year, or a history of blood transfusions or needle sticks in the past year.
